title: Curiosity before judgement: one question that changes the story
description: The colleague who went quiet, the neighbour who parked badly, the friend who cancelled again. Before the verdict, one curious question can rewrite the whole story.

body.heading: The verdict arrives first
paragraphs: Minds are fast prosecutors. Someone cuts a queue, cancels a plan or answers shortly, and a complete story is filed within seconds — rude, lazy, doesn't care. The story feels like an observation, but it is mostly invention: we saw one act and supplied the entire character behind it.
The trouble is that the invented story then runs the relationship. We respond to the person we imagined, not the one in front of us, and they can feel the verdict even when we never say it aloud.

body.heading: Insert one question
paragraphs: Curiosity before judgement means pausing for a single question: what else could be true here? The quiet colleague may be carrying bad news. The cancelling friend may be ashamed of the reason. The badly parked neighbour may have been rushing to a hospital.

You do not have to believe the kind explanation, or excuse behaviour that genuinely harms. You only have to notice that your first story was one draft among several — and that acting on an unverified draft is how small moments become lasting rifts.

body.heading: When it matters, ask for real
paragraphs: With people who matter, curiosity can graduate into an actual question, asked gently and without a trap inside it: 'You've seemed quiet this week — is everything alright?' Sometimes the answer changes everything. Sometimes there is no answer, and the asking itself was the kindness.
Judgement will still arrive first; it always does. The skill is not silencing it. It is refusing to let it have the final word.

takeaway: Before acting on your first story about someone, ask what else could be true — curiosity does not excuse harm, but it stops invented verdicts running real relationships.
